Akathisia is an inner restlessness that drives repetitive movement, and the
movement usually fails to relieve it. That failure is the part worth
explaining, and accounts pitched at the receptor do not on their own explain
it. I am building an active inference account alongside them, which asks
whether the disorder sits in how bodily prediction errors are turned into
action rather than in the motor system itself.

## The syndrome has two halves {.k-head}

Braude, Barnes and Gore went through consecutive psychiatric admissions in 1983
and put the clinical features through a principal components analysis. The
features did not collapse onto one dimension. There is what the patient
reports, an inner restlessness that sitting still does not settle, and there is
what an observer sees, the weight shifting and the rocking.

Barnes built the rating scale around that split six years later. It scores the
objective movement and the subjective distress on separate items, and then asks
for a global judgement on top of both. A scale is a theory about what it
measures, and this one commits to the two halves being distinct enough to score
apart.

The commitment has a name for the case where they come apart completely.
Pseudoakathisia is the movement with the report missing. Miller and
Fleischhacker's review treats the subjective and the objective components as
separable throughout, and their prevalence figures show how much the definition
does: estimates run from 5 percent to nearly 37 percent depending on which half
of the syndrome is being counted and how strictly.

That range is the reason the question interests me. A receptor account predicts
a dose of movement disorder. It does not, on its own, say why the felt and the
seen should be able to occur without each other.

## It did not go away with the newer drugs {.k-head}

Demyttenaere and colleagues pooled the trials of antipsychotics licensed more
recently and found a weighted incidence of 7.7 percent. Lower than the figures
from the first-generation era, and not close to zero.

The treatment evidence points somewhere odd. Gerolymos and colleagues ran a
network meta-analysis of what actually works against antipsychotic-induced
akathisia, and the drugs that beat placebo were mirtazapine (SMD −1.20),
biperiden (−1.01), vitamin B6 (−0.92) and propranolol (−0.78). One
serotonergic, one anticholinergic, one cofactor, one beta blocker. Not a
dopamine agent among them. Pringsheim and colleagues reach a similar place in
the Canadian guideline, where the recommendations are mostly about withdrawing
or reducing the offending drug and then reaching for agents that are not aimed
at D2.

None of that refutes a dopaminergic account, and the drug that causes the
problem is a dopaminergic drug. But a syndrome whose two components dissociate,
whose reported frequency depends on which component you count, and which
responds to four drugs with four different targets, is a syndrome where the
level of description is worth arguing about.
